The city lights were buzzing with an artificial glow that made the stars seem like forgotten memories, a topic that held little significance to Arthur as he hurried into the café. He had chosen this place specifically because it allowed him to dine alone, a luxury he cherished. As he sat, he felt a flutter in his stomach—not from hunger, but from the anticipation of his true mission.

He pulled out a notebook, his pen poised for the act of writing, though he wasn’t composing an article. He was, as Jay Rayner had suggested, a spy. His target sat three tables away, buried in a book. Arthur leaned forward, his nose wrinkled slightly as he adjusted his glasses to get a better view. He wasn't looking for a romantic date, but rather observing the quiet dignity of the stranger who reminded him of the care workers he’d read about that morning—people who understood that the human spirit required care, not just sustenance. He watched the man sip his coffee and felt a strange, quiet connection to the simple, daily rituals of a life observed from afar.
